analysis.one_liner: Gives TSA screeners the same job rights, pay rules, and union bargaining as other federal workers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 137 cosponsors, including 12 Republicans, but was referred to two committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Transportation Security Administration officers are federal employees, but they work under a separate personnel system created after 9/11 that gives them fewer job protections, different pay rules, and more limited union bargaining rights than other federal workers. This bill would move them into the standard federal personnel system (Title 5 of the U.S. Code), guaranteeing no pay cuts in the transition, preserving accrued leave, extending law-enforcement availability pay and overtime protections to air marshals, and locking in national-level collective bargaining for screeners. It also orders audits of TSA recruitment, promotion equity, and workplace harassment and assault. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: TSA transportation security officers, federal air marshals, and TSA inspectors gain the standard federal job protections: formal grievance and appeal rights, merit-based discipline rules, locality-based pay parity with other federal workers, preserved leave, and collective bargaining at the national level with the union certified in 2011. Travelers gain indirectly if more stable staffing and lower turnover improve checkpoint screening, which the bill's own findings (Comptroller General reviews of recruitment, promotion, and harassment) are designed to probe.
analysis.who_benefits_short: TSA screeners, air marshals, and inspectors

how_it_helps.text: Converts all TSA employees and positions to the standard federal personnel system under Title 5 of the U.S. Code no later than December 31, 2024, repealing the separate authorities created under the Aviation and Transportation Security Act.

Applies federal labor-management relations (chapter 71) and adverse-action and grievance procedures (chapter 77) to screening agents within 90 days, and keeps screening agents eligible to form a collective bargaining unit with the union certified by the Federal Labor Relations Authority in 2011.

Guarantees no reduction in pay or law enforcement availability pay during conversion, credits TSA service toward General Schedule step placement, and directs a retirement-pay proposal for employees retiring within three years of conversion.

Extends law enforcement availability pay and Fair Labor Standards Act-comparable overtime to TSA federal air marshals, and preserves accrued leave, split-shift differentials, part-time premium pay, and group retention incentives.

Requires the Comptroller General to report on TSA recruitment, promotion equity and leadership diversity, and protections against workplace harassment and assault, and requires a congressional briefing on assaults and threats by the public against screeners.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of aligning TSA pay, premium pay, and payroll systems with Title 5; the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate attached. TSA and DHS leadership give up unilateral control over personnel policies, pay systems, and discipline, and security critics of the standard system argue national-level bargaining can slow adjustments at checkpoints; the bill attempts to answer this by freezing personnel changes during transition, requiring congressional notification of any new or emergency-related policy, and expressly preserving the federal prohibition on strikes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and TSA management discretion

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes appropriations of unspecified sums to carry out the conversion, and parity with General Schedule pay and locality adjustments would raise federal personnel costs; no cost estimate accompanied the introduced text.

During the transition the bill freezes most TSA personnel rules and requires new policies to be reported to Congress within 7 days, which constrains management flexibility, though it carves out modifications for emerging transportation security threats, national emergencies, and public health threats.

Moving to Title 5 does not give screeners the right to strike; the bill expressly preserves the federal statutes barring strikes against the government, so the leverage gained is grievance, appeal, and bargaining rights only.

The bill requires national-level bargaining for covered units, with local bargaining only by mutual consent of the union and the Federal Security Director, which consolidates negotiating power at the national level rather than at individual airports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: standard federal job protections and national bargaining rights for roughly the TSA frontline workforce, at a cost to taxpayers of pay parity and system conversion, and at a cost to management of some unilateral flexibility. The bill tries to limit security risk by preserving no-strike rules, emergency-policy carve-outs, and congressional notification requirements, and it protects current employees from pay cuts. The main honest objection is cost and transition complexity, not a loss of screening capability; the bill contains no provision changing screening procedures themselves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Homeland Security and Oversight committees the day it was introduced, then referred to a Homeland Security subcommittee, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) introduced the bill on May 14, 2024, with 15 original cosponsors including 5 Republicans, and it was referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and, in addition, the Committee on Oversight and Accountability.
The same day, it was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security; no further action appears in the legislative record for the remainder of the Congress.
By the end of the Congress the bill had 137 cosponsors, 125 Democrats and 12 Republicans.
Neither the House Homeland Security Committee nor the Oversight Committee reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor for a vote before the 118th Congress expired on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: TSA and DHS leadership kept the existing separate personnel system, with unilateral control over pay rules, policies, and discipline, and taxpayers avoided the conversion costs; the roughly TSA frontline workforce gained nothing because the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TSA management and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Bennie G. Thompson
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MS), lead sponsor, Homeland Security Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Rights for the TSA Workforce Act of 2024 on May 14, 2024, and recruited 15 original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 137 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill broad if lopsidedly Democratic support in the House.

for.name: American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE)
for.role: Union representing TSA officers (certified as the screeners' bargaining representative in 2011)
for.what_they_did: Long publicly campaigned for Title 5 personnel rights and full collective bargaining for TSA officers, the change this bill would enact.

against.name: House Republican leadership and committee chairs
against.role: Majority party controlling the House calendar and the Homeland Security and Oversight committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup of the bill in either committee and never brought it to the floor; no action followed the May 14, 2024 referrals for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 125 of 137 cosponsors — with 12 Republicans joining, while the Republican majority controlling the House calendar and the two referred committees took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: TSA transportation security workforce (screeners, air marshals, inspectors)
industries.note: The bill gives these roughly tens of thousands of federal employees the standard Title 5 job protections, grievance and appeal rights, pay parity, and national collective bargaining that other federal workers have. Their working conditions are also the public's screening security, so more stable staffing and lower turnover serve travelers too.

Agency leadership loses the unilateral personnel authority created after 9/11: most existing personnel rules are frozen, new policies must be reported to Congress within 7 days, and discipline, grievances, and bargaining move into the standard federal framework. Management keeps carve-outs for emerging security threats, but its discretion is materially reduced.

The bill makes the union certified in 2011 the exclusive bargaining representative for screening agents under chapter 71 with national-level bargaining, a long-sought expansion of the union's role and membership base.

The conversion to Title 5 pay parity, premium pay, and system changes carries an unspecified cost authorized as 'such sums as may be necessary'; taxpayers fund it, while the workforce stability the bill seeks is intended to support screening quality for the traveling public.
